My thanks to Scott for digging this up for me.  I'm putting it up almost
unchanged, but I should point out that Shadow had some interesting feedback
on the commune movement.  My take on the sites that I looked at in
conjunction with her post was that many of them were religious communities,
but there are instances - one she cited on the Atlantic seaboard, more or
less, and the Hog Farm up in Oregon for two - that are longstanding and
currently self-sustaining communes.

Ex. 21:22-25 is often very incompletely read by many of the those who

"If, when men come to blows, they hurt a woman who is pregnant and she

However, I do *not* agree with the contention that the Bible is at best

drawn attention to by the Manifesto.  The argument "oh, well  the Bible
got written a long time ago" evades several things:  there are instances
- nowhere near 100%, but certainly instances - where events mentioned in
the Bible refer to things which actually happened.

We know, for instance, that the New Testament does in fact refer to
Roman functionaries actually serving, from other sources.  We know that

results of the archeology adjacent to the site.  Many of the migrations
of peoples as discussed in the Old Testament did in fact occur;  the
Bible may well be <ahem> elaborating considerably in its depictions of
their motives and their actions, but it remains the sole source for
descriptions of some of those.

Much of what Kaczynski argues in the Manifesto cannot be objectively
shown to be true, valid or useful.  We���ve seen it recently to be
subjectively true - Shadow experiences it as truth in her life, while
Paul Cox experiences it as false.  From a subjective point of view, the
Bible can���t just be dismissed out of hand as easily as some here would
- it has, after all, lots of subscribers.  It���s also a very important
thing in cultural history and mythology - far more so, I think even
Shadow���d agree - than the Manifesto.

Para 29:  Where does this line of reasoning extend to?  TK seems to be
arguing that the scholastic and economic inequalities which were

somehow essential to the maintenance of blackness.

What would he say to a Paul Robeson?  (For those of you who don���t know:
Princeton football star and Cum Laude grad in the 20���s;  law school

Indeed, one of the Buddhist sutras is the story of a woman who visits
the Buddha, distraught over the loss of one of her children.  Can the
Buddha resurrect her child?  The Buddha will, but first she must travel
until she meets a family untouched by such a tragedy.  She spends a year
traveling the countryside, and of course discovers that she cannot find
such a family.  When she returns to the Buddha, she���s understood that
all families are struck, and all grieve.  She still grieves;  only
Buddha was able to be nonattached - it is a condition which comes with
being Enlightened, not from the ordinary experience of disease and
death. (And remember, this sutra was first doing its important religious
work ca. 2000 years ago, and in a part of the world where our leaders
would like us to believe that "life is valued less than it is here."
Apparently not, since this is an important enough sutra to have survived
the span of time.)

Para 87:  The Motives of Scientists.  I found this section to be
particularly weak.  I think that again, because of his isolation even
when he was in an academic setting, he didn���t give sufficient weight to
the notion that there are people who really are just curious, and get a
great deal of satisfaction from engaging that curiosity.

For instance, the two best-read science publications are probably Nature
and Science magazines.  Most of the people I know who read them spend as
much or more time looking over the survey articles at the front of the
magazine on topics wholly unrelated to their own research as they do on the
one or two papers in an issue which may be directly relevant to their work.
For instance, I find the current debates over the mass and rate of
expansion of the universe, and the question of whether it will eventually
be able to reverse its rate of expansion and collapse in on itself
incredibly interesting.  I don���t have the background to read the research
on the topic, so I read the surveys for a general readership instead.

One of the things I value most about working in a setting where there
are people around who���ve read the same reviews is just bullshitting
about them.

So when TK asserts:  "Is the chemist curious about the appropriate
classification of a new species of beetle? No," he may well be wrong.
If the classification of the species of beetle is written carefully
about and the relevance of that assignment is made clear, it may well be
engaging to lots of people.  Stephen Gould has made a tidy living from
explaining the relationships of extinct snails, his specialty, to the
general public, for goodness��� sake!  (Of course, he's also gone farther
afield.)

Para 92:  ���This is interesting;  he essentially denies moral agency to
scientists.  A letter published this week in Nature from a group of
people working on the Convention on Biological Diversity points out
"Whether or not this protocol will provide for the consideration of
social and economic issues is as yet undecided."  This point is made
critically - the authors of the letter are imploring the larger
community of scientists to make that consideration an *explicit* goal
because they recognize that as it now stands, it is an *implicit* goal
and they are required to consider it but not voice their considerations.

They are asking to be able to voice these "broader social implications"
explicitly.  They recognize that they are now being given an ethical
agency, and that they need to be able to act on it in the open.

In talking with people who I think have worked in what are to me
genuinely negative fields of research - weapons design at Lawrence
Livermore, for instance - I find that those who are directing and
actively engaged in the work are there because they think they are doing
the right thing for the country, even with all the risks their work
entails, and that by doing the right thing for the country, they do the
right thing for the world.  These people are actively aware of and
engaging their moral agency - in a direction which I choose not to.

The people who seem unwilling to do so are bright people who act more in
support than in directing the work.  They see employment in the field as
ethically neutral, as just a legal job, and don���t like thinking about
the costs and benefits of the work.
